What is Bash: Bash (Bourne Again SHell) is a Unix shell and command language written by Brian Fox for the GNU Project. It's the default shell on most Linux distributions and macOS. Bash interprets commands, runs programs, and supports scripting with variables, control flow, and functions.

#!/bin/bash
# This is a Bash script

echo "Hello from Bash!"

# Check your shell
echo "Current shell: $SHELL"

# Bash version
bash --version
Terminal vs Shell: A terminal (or terminal emulator) is the graphical window where you type commands. A shell (like Bash) is the program inside that terminal that interprets your commands. The terminal sends your keystrokes to the shell, and the shell sends output back to the terminal.

# Common terminal emulators: GNOME Terminal, Konsole, iTerm2, Windows Terminal
# Common shells: bash, zsh, fish, sh

# See what shell you're running
echo $0

# See available shells
cat /etc/shells
Navigating the Filesystem: pwd prints your current directory. ls lists directory contents. cd changes directory. Use absolute paths (starting with /) or relative paths. ~ is your home directory, . is current directory, .. is parent directory.

# Where am I?
pwd

# List files
ls
ls -la          # detailed view with hidden files
ls -lh          # human-readable sizes

# Navigate
cd /tmp         # absolute path
cd ~            # home directory
cd ..           # parent directory
cd -            # previous directory
man & Help: man displays the system manual for any command. Use q to quit, / to search, n/N for next/prev match. Most commands also support --help or -h for a quick usage summary. info provides more detailed documentation.

# Get manual pages
man ls
man bash

# Quick help
grep --help
ls --help

# Search manual pages by keyword
man -k search
man -k "list files"
Basic Commands Overview: Essential commands: echo (print text), date (show date/time), whoami (current user), id (user info), uname (system info), uptime (system uptime), cal (calendar), clear (clear terminal), history (command history), hostname (system hostname).

echo "Hello World"
date
whoami
id
uname -a
uphone
cal 2025
history | tail -10
hostname

Creating & Deleting Files: touch creates empty files or updates timestamps. rm removes files. Use -i for confirmation, -f to force, -r for directories. Be careful — rm -rf is powerful and dangerous. mkdir creates directories, rmdir removes empty directories.

# File operations
touch file.txt
rm file.txt
rm -i file.txt    # prompt before remove

# Directory operations
mkdir mydir
mkdir -p parent/child/grandchild   # create intermediate dirs
rmdir mydir                         # only empty dirs
rm -rf mydir                        # remove recursively (dangerous!)
Copying & Moving: cp copies files and directories. mv moves or renames files. Both accept -i (interactive), -v (verbose), -u (update newer). For directories, cp needs -r (recursive). mv always works on directories without extra flags.

# Copy
cp source.txt dest.txt
cp -i source.txt dest.txt    # prompt before overwrite
cp -r mydir /backup/mydir    # copy directory recursively

# Move/Rename
mv oldname.txt newname.txt
mv file.txt /tmp/            # move to another directory
mv -i file.txt dest.txt      # prompt before overwrite
Linking Files: ln creates links. Hard links are multiple directory entries pointing to the same inode — deleting one doesn't affect others. Soft links (symlinks) are pointers to another path — they break if the target is moved or deleted. Symbolic links can cross filesystems.

# Hard link
ln target.txt hardlink.txt
ls -li          # same inode number

# Symbolic link
ln -s target.txt symlink.txt
ls -la          # shows -> target

# Symlinks can point to directories
ln -s /usr/bin binlink

# Broken symlink (target deleted)
rm target.txt
cat symlink.txt  # No such file or directory
Finding Files: find searches the filesystem by name, type, size, date, and more. locate uses a prebuilt database for faster searches but may be stale. which shows the path of an executable. whereis finds binary, source, and man pages.

# find: powerful but slower
find /home -name "*.txt"
find . -type f -size +1M
find . -mtime -7              # modified in last 7 days
find . -name "*.log" -delete  # find and delete

# locate: fast but uses database
sudo updatedb                  # update database first
locate bashrc

# which & whereis
which python3
whereis bash
File Attributes & stat: stat displays detailed file metadata: size, blocks, permissions, timestamps (access, modify, change), and inode number. file detects the file type by examining magic bytes. du estimates file/directory size usage.

# File metadata
stat file.txt
stat -c "%s bytes, permissions %A" file.txt

# Detect file type
file mystery.bin
file *

# Disk usage
du -sh mydir          # total size
du -ah mydir          # per-file sizes
du --max-depth=1 /home

cat & less: cat concatenates and displays files. Use it for small files or joining files. less is a pager for viewing large files with scroll, search, and navigation. less is better than cat for files longer than one screen. Use q to quit less.

# cat for small files or joining
cat file.txt
cat file1.txt file2.txt > combined.txt
cat -n file.txt              # with line numbers

# less for paging
less largefile.log
# Inside less: /search, n/N, g/G, q
head & tail: head shows the first N lines (default 10) of a file. tail shows the last N lines. tail -f follows a file as it grows — essential for monitoring logs. Both support -n for line count and -c for byte count.

# First/last lines
head file.txt
head -n 20 file.txt
head -c 100 file.txt         # first 100 bytes

tail file.txt
tail -n 50 file.txt
tail -f /var/log/syslog      # follow mode (Ctrl+C to stop)

# View lines 50-60
head -n 60 file.txt | tail -n 11
nano & vim Basics: nano is a beginner-friendly terminal text editor with on-screen shortcuts. vim is a powerful modal editor with multiple modes: Normal (navigation), Insert (editing), Visual (selection), and Command (ex commands). Learn vim for speed; use nano for simplicity.

# nano — simple, intuitive
nano file.txt
# ^O save, ^X exit, ^W search, ^K cut, ^U paste

# vim — powerful, modal
vim file.txt
# i = insert mode, Esc = normal mode
# :w save, :q quit, :wq save & quit
# /search, n/N next/prev, dd delete line
Viewing Binary & Special Files: hexdump (hd), xxd, and od display binary file contents in hexadecimal, octal, or ASCII. strings extracts printable strings from binary files. Use these for debugging binary formats or examining executables.

# Hex dump
hexdump file.bin
xxd file.bin
od -c file.bin               # octal dump

# Extract strings from binary
strings /bin/ls | head -20
strings program.bin | grep -i error

grep — Search Text: grep searches files for patterns using regular expressions. Common options: -i (ignore case), -r (recursive), -v (invert match), -n (line numbers), -l (filename only), -c (count matches), -E (extended regex), -o (only matching).

# Basic usage
grep "error" log.txt
grep -ri "TODO" src/          # recursive, case-insensitive
grep -rn "function" .

# Advanced
grep -E "foo|bar" file.txt   # extended regex (alternation)
grep -v "^#" config.conf     # remove comments
grep -c "ERROR" log.txt      # count matches
grep -l "main" *.py          # filenames only

# Pipe with other commands
ps aux | grep python
dmesg | grep -i error | tail
sed — Stream Editor: sed processes and transforms text non-interactively. Most common: s/old/new/g (substitute), /pattern/d (delete), -n 'p' (print). sed supports in-place editing with -i. It works line-by-line by default.

# Substitution
sed 's/foo/bar/' file.txt          # first occurrence per line
sed 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt         # all occurrences
sed -i 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt      # in-place

# Line operations
sed '5d' file.txt                  # delete line 5
sed '/^#/d' file.txt               # delete comments
sed -n '10,20p' file.txt           # print lines 10-20

# Multiple commands
sed -e 's/foo/bar/' -e 's/baz/qux/' file.txt
awk — Text Processing: awk is a powerful text-processing language for field-based data. Default field separator is whitespace. $0 is the whole line, $1, $2, etc. are fields. Supports patterns, actions, and built-in variables (NF, NR, FS, OFS).

# Field extraction
awk '{print $1}' file.txt          # first column
awk '{print $1, $3}' file.txt

# With patterns
awk '/error/ {print $0}' log.txt   # lines matching error
awk '$3 > 50 {print $1}' data.txt  # conditional

# Built-in variables
awk '{print NR, $0}' file.txt      # line numbers
awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd   # colon separator

# Calculations
awk '{sum += $1} END {print sum}' numbers.txt
cut, sort, uniq: cut extracts columns by delimiter (-d, -f). sort sorts lines alphabetically or numerically (-n), reverse (-r), unique (-u). uniq removes adjacent duplicates (use sort first). wc counts lines/words/characters.

# cut — extract columns
cut -d: -f1,3 /etc/passwd
cut -c1-10 file.txt              # characters 1-10

# sort
sort file.txt
sort -n numbers.txt               # numeric sort
sort -k2 -t: data.txt             # sort by 2nd field

# uniq
sort file.txt | uniq
sort file.txt | uniq -c           # count occurrences
sort file.txt | uniq -d           # only duplicates

# wc — word count
wc file.txt                       # lines, words, chars
wc -l file.txt                    # line count only
tr & diff: tr translates or deletes characters (from stdin only). Usage: tr 'set1' 'set2'. diff compares files line by line. comm compares sorted files for common/unique lines.

# tr — translate/delete
echo "hello" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'    # uppercase
echo "hello" | tr -d 'l'          # delete all 'l'
echo "a b c" | tr -s ' '         # squeeze spaces

# diff — compare files
diff file1.txt file2.txt
diff -u file1.txt file2.txt       # unified format

# comm — compare sorted files
comm file1.txt file2.txt
comm -12 file1.txt file2.txt      # common lines only

Understanding Permissions: Linux file permissions: r (read=4), w (write=2), x (execute=1). Three tiers: owner (u), group (g), others (o). ls -l shows permissions as -rwxr-xr--. The first character indicates file type (-=file, d=dir, l=symlink).

# View permissions
ls -l
# -rwxr-xr--
# |||||||||
# ||||||||+-- others: read
# |||||||+--- others: no execute
# ||||||+---- group: read
# |||||+----- group: execute
# ||||+------ group: no write
# |||+------- owner: read
# ||+-------- owner: write
# |+--------- owner: execute
# +---------- file type (-)
chmod — Change Permissions: chmod changes file permissions using symbolic (u+x, g-w, o=r) or octal (755, 644) modes. Common settings: 755 (rwxr-xr-x) for directories/executables, 644 (rw-r--r--) for files. Use -R for recursive.

# Symbolic mode
chmod +x script.sh          # add execute to all
chmod u+x script.sh         # add execute to owner only
chmod go-w file.txt         # remove write from group & others

# Octal mode
chmod 755 script.sh         # rwxr-xr-x
chmod 644 file.txt          # rw-r--r--
chmod 600 secret.txt       # rw-------

# Recursive
chmod -R 755 mydir/
chown & chgrp: chown changes file owner and group. chgrp changes group only. Syntax: chown user:group file. Use -R for recursive. Only root can change ownership; a user can chgrp to groups they belong to.

# Change owner
sudo chown alice file.txt
sudo chown alice:admin file.txt
sudo chown :admin file.txt         # change group only

# Recursive
sudo chown -R alice:users /home/alice

# chgrp
chgrp developers project/
chgrp -R developers shared/
umask & Default Permissions: umask sets default permissions for new files and directories. It subtracts from the base permissions (666 for files, 777 for dirs). Common: umask 022 = 644/755, umask 077 = 600/700. Set it in .bashrc.

# Check current umask
umask
# 0022

# Common umask values
umask 022    # files: 644, dirs: 755 (default)
umask 077    # files: 600, dirs: 700 (private)
umask 002    # files: 664, dirs: 775 (group writable)

# Test
umask 077
touch test.txt
ls -l test.txt   # -rw-------
sudo & Root Access: sudo executes a command as another user (default root). sudo -i opens a root shell. visudo edits /etc/sudoers safely. /etc/sudoers.d/ contains drop-in configs. The sudoers file controls who can run what commands.

# Basic usage
sudo apt update
sudo -u alice whoami       # run as alice
sudo -i                    # root shell

# Run previous command with sudo
sudo !!                    # !! = last command

# sudoers config (edit with visudo)
# user ALL=(ALL) ALL
# %admin ALL=(ALL) ALL
# alice ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/apt
Special Permissions: SUID (setuid, 4xxx) runs a program with the file owner's privileges. SGID (setgid, 2xxx) runs with group privileges — on directories, new files inherit the group. Sticky bit (1xxx, chmod +t) prevents non-owners from deleting files in shared directories (/tmp).

# Set SUID — runs as owner
chmod u+s /usr/bin/program
chmod 4755 script          # rwsr-xr-x

# Set SGID on directory — new files inherit group
chmod g+s shared_dir/
chmod 2775 shared_dir      # rwxrwsr-x

# Sticky bit — only owner can delete
chmod +t /shared
chmod 1777 /tmp            # rwxrwxrwt

# Check special permissions
ls -la /usr/bin/passwd     # rwsr-xr-x (SUID)
ls -ld /tmp                # drwxrwxrwt (sticky)

Viewing Processes: ps lists running processes. Common: ps aux (all users, detailed), ps ef (full-format), ps -eo (custom format). top shows real-time process info. htop is an interactive alternative (install separately). Uptime shows system load averages.

# Process listing
ps aux
ps aux --sort=-%mem          # sorted by memory
ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd,%mem,%cpu --sort=-%cpu

# Real-time monitoring
top
htop                         # prettier (install first)

# System load
uphone
# load average: 1min, 5min, 15min
Managing Processes: kill sends signals to processes. Common signals: SIGTERM (15, graceful), SIGKILL (9, force), SIGHUP (1, reload). killall kills by name. pkill kills by pattern. pgrep finds PIDs by name.

# Kill by PID
kill 1234                    # SIGTERM (default)
kill -9 1234                 # SIGKILL (force)
kill -15 1234                # SIGTERM (explicit)

# Kill by name
killall nginx
pkill -f "python server.py"

# Find PIDs
pgrep -u alice
pidof nginx

# Reload config
kill -HUP $(pgrep nginx)
Background & Foreground Jobs: Appending & runs a command in the background. Ctrl+Z suspends the foreground job. bg resumes a suspended job in the background. fg brings a job to the foreground. jobs lists background jobs. disown detaches a job from the shell.

# Background a command
sleep 100 &

# Suspend foreground (Ctrl+Z), then background
sleep 100
# Press Ctrl+Z
bg

# Manage jobs
jobs
fg %1                       # bring job 1 to foreground

# Detach from shell (survive logout)
sleep 100 &
disown

# nohup — immune to hangup
nohup longscript.sh &
Systemd & Services: systemctl manages systemd services. Common: start, stop, restart, enable, disable, status. service is the legacy command. systemd units are defined in .service files in /etc/systemd/system/ and /lib/systemd/system/.

# Managing services
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl stop nginx
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo systemctl status nginx

# Enable at boot
sudo systemctl enable nginx
sudo systemctl disable nginx

# View all services
systemctl list-units --type=service
systemctl list-unit-files | grep enabled

# Journalctl — view logs
journalctl -u nginx
journalctl -u nginx -f          # follow mode

Standard Streams: Three standard streams: stdin (0, input), stdout (1, output), stderr (2, errors). By default, stdin comes from keyboard, stdout/stderr go to terminal. Redirection changes where these streams point. < redirects stdin, > redirects stdout.

# Output redirection
ls > files.txt               # stdout to file (overwrite)
echo "hello" >> log.txt     # stdout to file (append)

# Input redirection
sort < unsorted.txt

# Error redirection
ls /nonexistent 2> error.log
command 2>> error.log        # append stderr

# Redirect both stdout and stderr
command &> output.txt
command > output.txt 2>&1    # traditional syntax
Pipes: Pipes (|) connect stdout of one command to stdin of another. This creates powerful command chains called pipelines. Each command runs in parallel. The exit status of a pipeline is that of the last command (pipefail option changes this).

# Basic pipe
ls -la | grep ".txt"

# Multi-stage pipeline
ps aux | grep python | grep -v grep | awk '{print $2}'

# Count files
ls | wc -l

# Readable disk usage
df -h | grep -v tmpfs | sort -k5 -rn

# Complex pipeline
cat log.txt | grep ERROR | cut -d' ' -f1-3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Here Documents & Strings: Here documents (<< EOF) pass multi-line input to a command until a delimiter. Here strings (<<<) pass a single string as stdin. These are especially useful in scripts for providing inline input to commands.

# Here document
cat << EOF
This is a
multi-line
message
EOF

# Here document with variables
name="Alice"
cat << EOF
Hello, $name
EOF

# Quoted delimiter prevents variable expansion
cat << 'EOF'
$variable will NOT expand
EOF

# Here string
grep "error" <<< "no errors here"
tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' <<< "hello"
Process Substitution: Process substitution <(command) or >(command) treats command output as a file. Useful for diffing command outputs or passing multiple inputs. Available in bash but not POSIX sh.

# Compare outputs of two commands
diff <(ls dir1) <(ls dir2)

# Pass multiple inputs to a command
comm <(sort file1) <(sort file2)

# Read from a command as if it's a file
while read line; do
    echo "$line"
done < <(grep "TODO" src/**/*.js)

# Redirect output to a process
ls > >(gzip > output.gz)
tee & xargs: tee reads stdin and writes to both stdout and files (like a T-pipe). Useful for logging while still seeing output. xargs reads items from stdin and executes a command with them. Essential for batch operations.

# tee — split output
ls -la | tee listing.txt           # print and save
command | tee log.txt | grep error
command | tee -a log.txt           # append mode

# xargs — build and execute commands
find . -name "*.tmp" | xargs rm -f
echo "a b c" | xargs mkdir        # create multiple dirs

# xargs with placeholder
find . -name "*.jpg" | xargs -I{} cp {} /backup/{}

# Parallel execution
xargs -P 4 -n 1 command < tasks.txt

Shebang & Execution: The shebang (#!) on the first line tells the kernel which interpreter to use. Make scripts executable with chmod +x. Run with ./script.sh or bash script.sh. Arguments are $1, $2, ..., $0 is the script name.

#!/bin/bash
# Save as hello.sh

echo "Script name: $0"
echo "First arg: $1"
echo "All args: $@"
echo "Arg count: $#"

# Make executable:
# chmod +x hello.sh
# ./hello.sh World
Variables: Variables are assigned with name=value (no spaces). Read with $name or ${name}. Always quote variables ("$var") to prevent word splitting and globbing. Use readonly to make variables immutable, unset to remove them.

#!/bin/bash
name="Alice"
age=30

echo "$name is $age years old"
echo "${name}_file.txt"           # brace for clarity

# Always quote!
path="/path/with spaces"
ls "$path"                         # works
ls $path                            # breaks

# readonly & unset
readonly PI=3.14159
unset age                           # delete variable
Expansions & Substitutions: Bash supports several expansions: brace ({a,b,c}), tilde (~), parameter ($var, ${var:-default}), command ($(cmd)), and arithmetic ($((expr))). Expansion happens in a specific order before the command executes.

# Brace expansion
echo {a,b,c}.txt              # a.txt b.txt c.txt
touch file-{1..5}.txt

# Command substitution
now=$(date)
echo "Today is $now"
files=$(ls | wc -l)

# Arithmetic
echo $((2 + 2))
echo $((x * 10))

# Parameter expansion
name=${name:-"default"}       # use default if unset
name=${name:?"error message"} # error if unset
Quoting: Single quotes preserve every character literally. Double quotes preserve most but allow $, ``, \, and ! expansion. Backslash escapes the next character. ANSI-C quoting ($'...') interprets escape sequences like \n, \t.

# Single quotes — literal
echo 'Hello $USER'            # $USER not expanded

# Double quotes — partial expansion
echo "Hello $USER"            # $USER expanded

# Escape characters
echo "Price: \$5"             # escaped dollar sign
echo He said \"hello\"

# ANSI-C quoting
echo $'Line1\nLine2'
echo $'Tab\tseparated'

# $'' for escape sequences
printf '%s\n' $'color\tvalue'
Exit Codes: Every command returns an exit code (0 = success, 1-255 = failure). $? contains the exit code of the last command. Use && (run if success) and || (run if failure) for chaining. exit terminates a script with a code.

# Check exit code
ls /tmp
echo $?                        # 0 = success

ls /nonexistent
echo $?                        # non-zero = failure

# Chaining commands
make && ./run_tests             # run tests only if build succeeds
make || echo "Build failed!"

# In scripts
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "Error occurred"
    exit 1
fi

if/elif/else: if executes commands based on the exit status of a test command. test or [ ] evaluates conditions: numeric (-eq, -ne, -lt, -gt), string (=, !=, -z, -n), file (-f, -d, -e, -r, -w, -x). Use [[ ]] for extended bash tests with &&, ||, =~.

#!/bin/bash
score=85

if [ "$score" -ge 90 ]; then
    echo "Grade: A"
elif [ "$score" -ge 80 ]; then
    echo "Grade: B"
else
    echo "Needs improvement"
fi

# File tests
if [ -f "config.json" ]; then
    echo "Config exists"
fi

# Extended test [[ ]]
if [[ "$name" =~ ^A.* ]]; then
    echo "Name starts with A"
fi
for Loops: for iterates over a list of words, array elements, or command output. Use for ((expr; cond; incr)) for C-style loops. Use continue to skip iteration, break to exit early.

#!/bin/bash
# Iterate over list
for fruit in apple banana cherry; do
    echo "I like $fruit"
done

# Range
for i in {1..5}; do
    echo "Count: $i"
done

# C-style
for ((i=0; i<5; i++)); do
    echo "Number $i"
done

# Command output
for file in *.txt; do
    echo "Processing $file"
done
while & until Loops: while runs as long as the test command succeeds. until runs as long as the test command fails. Use read for line-by-line processing. Use break to exit, continue to skip iteration. watch out for infinite loops!

#!/bin/bash
# While loop
count=0
while [ "$count" -lt 5 ]; do
    echo "Count: $count"
    ((count++))
done

# Read file line by line
while IFS= read -r line; do
    echo "Line: $line"
done < file.txt

# Until loop
until ping -c1 google.com &>/dev/null; do
    echo "Waiting for network..."
    sleep 2
done

echo "Network is up!"
case Statement: case matches a value against patterns (like switch). Patterns can use *, ?, [...], and | for alternation. Each case ends with ;;. Use *) for default. esac ends the statement.
select Menu: select creates an interactive menu from a list of items. The user picks a number, and the selected item is stored in the variable. Combined with case for menu-driven scripts. Break out with Ctrl+D or an empty input.

#!/bin/bash
echo "Choose your favorite:"

select option in "JavaScript" "Python" "Go" "Rust" "Quit"; do
    case $option in
        "JavaScript")
            echo "Good choice!"
            ;;
        "Python")
            echo "Snake charmer!"
            ;;
        "Go"|"Rust")
            echo "Systems fan!"
            ;;
        "Quit")
            break
            ;;
        *)
            echo "Invalid option"
            ;;
    esac
done

Defining Functions: Functions group commands for reuse. Define with function name { } or name() { }. Use local for function-scoped variables. Functions return with return (0-255) or set an exit code. Declare -f lists defined functions.
Arrays: Bash supports indexed arrays (declare -a) and associative arrays (declare -A). Accessed with ${array[index]}. ${array[@]} expands all elements. ${#array[@]} gives length. Useful for lists and lookups.

#!/bin/bash
# Indexed array
fruits=("apple" "banana" "cherry")
echo "${fruits[0]}"              # apple
echo "${fruits[@]}"              # all elements
echo "${#fruits[@]}"             # length

# Add elements
fruits+=("date")

# Iterate
for fruit in "${fruits[@]}"; do
    echo "$fruit"
done

# Associative array (declare -A)
declare -A capitals
capitals[USA]="Washington"
capitals[UK]="London"
echo "${capitals[USA]}"
Argument Parsing with getopts: getopts parses command-line flags and options in scripts. Each option character can have a colon suffix to require an argument. OPTIND tracks the next argument index. Use a while loop with case for processing.
Error Handling & Trap: trap catches signals and executes commands. Common: trap 'cleanup' EXIT, trap 'handler' INT (Ctrl+C). set -e exits on error, set -u errors on undefined variables, set -o pipefail catches pipeline errors. Combined: set -euo pipefail.

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail            # strict mode

cleanup() {
    echo "Cleaning up..."
    rm -f /tmp/tempfile
}
trap cleanup EXIT            # always runs on exit

trap 'echo "Interrupted!"; exit 1' INT

echo "Working..."
sleep 10
echo "Done"
Debugging Scripts: bash -x script.sh prints each command before execution (xtrace). set -x enables within a script. PS4 customizes the trace prompt. bash -n script.sh checks syntax without running. bash -v prints input lines.

#!/bin/bash
# Enable debugging
set -x                        # trace commands
echo "Debugging this"
name="Alice"
echo "Hello $name"
set +x                        # disable tracing

# Run from CLI:
# bash -x script.sh
# bash -n script.sh    # syntax check only

# Custom PS4 for better traces
PS4='+ $LINENO: '
set -x

curl — HTTP Requests: curl transfers data using various protocols (HTTP, FTP, etc.). Common: curl URL (fetch), curl -o file (save), curl -O (save with filename), curl -I (headers only), curl -d (POST data), curl -H (custom header).

# GET request
curl https://api.example.com/users
curl -o output.json https://api.example.com/users

# Headers only
curl -I https://google.com

# POST with data
curl -X POST -d '{"name":"Alice"}' -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://api.example.com/users

# Download file
curl -O https://example.com/file.zip
curl -L -o myfile.zip https://bit.ly/short-url    # follow redirects
wget — Download Tool: wget is a non-interactive downloader supporting recursive downloads, resuming, and mirroring. Unlike curl, wget is designed for downloads and works well with -r (recursive), -c (resume), -m (mirror).

# Basic download
wget https://example.com/file.zip

# Resume interrupted download
wget -c https://example.com/largefile.zip

# Recursive download (limit depth)
wget -r -l2 https://example.com/docs/

# Mirror a website
wget -m -p -k https://example.com/

# Download with custom name
wget -O archive.zip https://example.com/download
ssh — Remote Access: SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted remote access. ssh user@host connects to a remote machine. Key-based auth with ssh-keygen + ssh-copy-id is more secure than passwords. ~/.ssh/config simplifies connections.

# Basic connection
ssh alice@server.example.com
ssh -p 2222 user@host         # custom port

# Key-based auth
ssh-keygen -t ed25519         # generate key pair
ssh-copy-id user@host         # copy public key

# SSH config (~/.ssh/config)
# Host myserver
#     HostName 192.168.1.100
#     User alice
#     Port 2222
#     IdentityFile ~/.ssh/mykey

# Run command remotely
ssh user@host "ls -la /var/log"
scp & rsync: scp securely copies files over SSH. rsync is a powerful sync tool that transfers only differences, supports compression (-z), archive mode (-a), and deletion (-delete). rsync is better for large or repeated transfers.

# scp — simple copy
scp file.txt user@host:/remote/path/
scp -r mydir/ user@host:/remote/path/
scp user@host:/remote/file.txt ./

# rsync — synchronized copy (preferred)
rsync -avz source/ user@host:/dest/          # archive, verbose, compress
rsync -avz --delete source/ user@host:/dest/ # remove extraneous files
rsync -n -avz source/ user@host:/dest/       # dry run

# Local sync
rsync -av /src/ /backup/
Network Diagnostics: ping tests host reachability. netstat (or ss) shows network connections, ports, and routing tables. ss is the modern replacement for netstat. dig/nslookup queries DNS. traceroute traces network path.

# Ping
ping -c 4 google.com

# Port/Socket info
ss -tuln                    # listening TCP/UDP ports
ss -tup                     # active connections
netstat -tuln               # traditional (install net-tools)

# DNS lookup
dig google.com
nslookup google.com
host google.com

# Trace route
traceroute google.com

# Bandwidth
iperf3 -c server.example.com

Bash Startup Files: .bashrc runs for interactive non-login shells. .bash_profile (or .profile) runs for login shells. .bash_logout runs on logout. On macOS, Terminal opens login shells (use .bash_profile). On Linux, terminals typically use .bashrc.

# ~/.bashrc — aliases, functions, prompt (interactive non-login)
# ~/.bash_profile — env vars, PATH (login shell)
# ~/.profile — fallback for sh-compatible shells

# Common pattern: source .bashrc from .bash_profile
if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then
    . ~/.bashrc
fi

# /etc/bash.bashrc — system-wide defaults
# /etc/profile — system-wide env vars
Aliases: Aliases create shorthand commands. List all aliases with alias (bare). Remove with unalias. Aliases don't accept arguments (use functions instead). Put aliases in .bashrc for persistence.

# Create aliases
alias ll='ls -la'
alias ..='cd ..'
alias gs='git status'
alias gc='git commit'
alias ..2='cd ../..'

# List aliases
alias

# Remove alias
unalias ll

# Bypass alias (use original command)
\ls
'ls'
command ls
Environment Variables: Environment variables are inherited by child processes. Set with export VAR=value. PATH controls where the shell looks for executables. Common: HOME, USER, SHELL, EDITOR, LANG, PATH, PS1. Add to .bashrc for persistence.

# Set & export
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
export EDITOR=nano
export LANG=en_US.UTF-8

# List all env vars
printenv
echo "$HOME $USER $SHELL"

# PATH management
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin"
export PATH="./node_modules/.bin:$PATH"

# Make variables available to children
export MY_VAR="value"
my_local="not exported"

# Unset
unset MY_VAR
PS1 Prompt Customization: PS1 defines the primary prompt. Use escape sequences: \u (user), \h (host), \w (working dir), \W (basename), \d (date), \t (time), \n (newline), \$ (# for root, $ otherwise). Set in .bashrc.

# Simple prompt
export PS1="\u@\h:\w\$ "

# With colors and git branch
export PS1='\[\e[32m\]\u@\h\[\e[00m\]:\[\e[34m\]\w\[\e[00m\]$(__git_ps1 " (%s)")\$ '

# Multi-line prompt
export PS1="\u@\h\n\w\$ "

# Test without changing file
PS1='\[\e[31m\]➜\[\e[00m\] '

# Add to .bashrc for permanence
echo 'export PS1="\u@\h:\w\$ "' >> ~/.bashrc
Command Completion: Bash programmable completion completes commands, filenames, and arguments. Complete with Tab (double Tab to show all). bash-completion package adds completion for git, ssh, apt, and hundreds of commands.

# Enable programmable completion (often in /etc/bash.bashrc)
if [ -f /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion ]; then
    . /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion
fi

# List loaded completions
complete -p

# Add custom completion for a function
_myfunc_complete() {
    local cur=${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD]}
    COMPREPLY=($(compgen -W "start stop restart status" -- "$cur"))
}
complete -F _myfunc_complete mycommand

cron — Scheduled Jobs: cron runs commands at scheduled times. crontab -e edits your user's crontab. Format: minute hour day month weekday command. Use */n for every n, commas for lists, hyphens for ranges. Cron output is emailed by default.

# Crontab format:
# ┌──────── minute (0-59)
# │ ┌──────── hour (0-23)
# │ │ ┌──────── day of month (1-31)
# │ │ │ ┌──────── month (1-12)
# │ │ │ │ ┌──────── day of week (0-7, 0/7=Sun)
# * * * * * command

# Edit crontab
crontab -e
crontab -l                    # list

# Examples:
# Every day at 6 AM
0 6 * * * /home/alice/backup.sh

# Every 30 minutes
*/30 * * * * /home/alice/check.sh

# Every weekday at 9 AM
0 9 * * 1-5 /home/alice/work.sh
at — One-Time Jobs: at schedules a command for a specific time (one-time). Use at now + 5 minutes, at 2 PM tomorrow, etc. atq lists pending jobs, atrm removes a job. Commands are read from stdin or piped.

# Schedule a job
echo "sh backup.sh" | at 2:00 PM
echo "rm /tmp/oldfiles/*" | at now + 1 hour

# Interactive mode
at 9:00 AM tomorrow
at> echo "Time to wake up" | mail alice
at> # Press Ctrl+D to submit

# Manage jobs
atq                           # list pending jobs
atrm 5                        # remove job id 5

# Batch — runs when system load is low
batch < job.sh
Writing Robust Scripts: Robust scripts handle errors, use strict mode, validate arguments, and log output. Always quote variables, check command success, provide usage messages, and clean up temp files. set -euo pipefail is essential.

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Usage check
if [ $# -lt 1 ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 <input-file> [output-dir]"
    exit 1
fi

INPUT="$1"
OUTPUT="${2:-./output}"

# Validate input
if [ ! -f "$INPUT" ]; then
    echo "Error: $INPUT not found"
    exit 1
fi

# Create output dir
mkdir -p "$OUTPUT"

# Log progress
echo "[$(date)] Processing $INPUT..." >> script.log

# Main work
echo "Processing..."

# Cleanup on exit
trap 'echo "Done with $INPUT" >> script.log' EXIT
